_comment: Source data for scripts/generate_teacher_guides.py. Level membership (GPCs, tricky words, exit criteria) is verbatim from output/worksheet_plan/CURRICULUM_LEDGER.md v2.1. Weekly rhythm text follows output/worksheet_plan/SCHOOL_SCHEME_RECEPTION_TO_Y2.md v1.1 exactly. 'group' on a spread = in-level unlock stage: words/dictation for a spread may use GPCs from any spread whose group <= this spread's group (mirrors the 2-GPCs-per-week condensed cycles at L1-L2 and the per-book sound pairs from L3). Validator note: the article 'a' is treated as readable from L1 (the grapheme a is taught in week 1); it is not printed in the tricky word lists, which stay verbatim to the ledger.

levels.name: Ditties
levels.decodable_rule: Every word must be a VC or CVC word formed from the 10 GPCs above, or one of the 2 listed tricky words. No consonant clusters. No digraphs. No double letters.
exit_criteria: Reads all 10 Phase 2 GPCs at sight
Blends VC and CVC words with confidence
Forms all 10 taught lower-case letters correctly from a model
Leaves finger spaces when copying a modelled sentence

term_map.teach: s a t p i n m d g o · oral blending · VC/CVC · I, the · first letter formation
term_map.secure: Blend and read CVC words from the first 10 GPCs; form all 10 letters

spreads.label: /s/ as in sun
spreads.note: In week one there is no code yet to blend with — the session is oral blending (s-u-n → sun) and formation. The words above become readable within days, once a, t and p are in.
spreads.errors: A continuous, hissy sound — hold it /sss/, never 'suh' (no added vowel). Formation: the snake curve is often reversed; start at the top.

spreads.label: /a/ as in apple
spreads.note: Teach the sound /a/, not the letter name — children who know the alphabet song will offer 'ay'.
spreads.errors: Letter-name interference ('ay' for /a/) is the classic error. Keep the mouth wide open — /a/ as in apple. Round-then-down formation, anticlockwise.

spreads.label: /t/ as in tap
spreads.errors: A sharp, bouncy sound — /t/, not 'tuh'. Down first, lift, then cross: children who cross first form it backwards. t is a shorty-with-a-hat, not a full ascender.

spreads.label: /p/ as in pat
spreads.note: pit becomes readable next week when i arrives.
spreads.errors: p/b voicing pair — /p/ is a puff of air with no voice. The descender goes below the line; expect b/d/p/q rotations for months. 'Down the pole, up and round' every time.

spreads.label: /i/ as in it
spreads.errors: The tightest vowel pair in English is /i/ v /e/ — /e/ arrives at Level 2, so anchor /i/ hard now (itchy i). Dot added after the down-stroke, not before.

spreads.label: /n/ as in nap
spreads.errors: n/m confusion — both nasal sounds, both bump letters. Count the bumps aloud while forming: n has one, m has two. Hold /nnn/ as a continuous sound.

spreads.label: /m/ as in mat
spreads.errors: A continuous humming sound — /mmm/, lips together, no 'muh'. Two bumps, both touching the line. m/n mix-ups persist in reading and writing.

spreads.label: /d/ as in dad
spreads.note: dig becomes readable next week when g arrives.
spreads.errors: THE reversal letter: b/d confusion is normal well into Year 1. Teach the formation route, not the shape — d starts like a, 'round first, then up, then down'. Never teach b and d in the same week.

spreads.label: /g/ as in gap
spreads.errors: g/k voicing pair — /g/ is voiced, at the back of the mouth. Descender letter: the tail must hook below the line or it reads as a. Single-storey g only (matches Andika and the books).

spreads.label: /o/ as in on
spreads.errors: Keep /o/ short and round — not 'oh' (the letter name). o/a confusion in writing when the join-up stroke is sloppy: close the circle every time.

levels.name: First Sounds
levels.decodable_rule: CVC and CVCC words using all single-letter GPCs and ck. Double-letter endings (ff, ll, ss) permitted. No vowel digraphs. No consonant digraphs except ck.
exit_criteria: Reads all 26 single-letter GPCs, ck, ff, ll and ss at sight
Reads the 7 cumulative tricky words at sight
Blends CVC and CVCC words with double-letter endings
Forms all 26 lower-case letters correctly from a model
Writes a simple sentence with capital letter, finger spaces and full stop

term_map.teach: c k ck e u r h b f ff · CVC across the wider code
term_map.secure: Read CVC with any single-letter GPC + ck

term_map.teach: l ll ss j v w x y z · no go to into is · capital letters, full stop
term_map.secure: All 26 letters + double-letter endings; simple sentence with capital and full stop

spreads.label: /k/ as in cat
spreads.errors: c and k make the same sound — teach c as the everyday spelling of /k/. Sharp sound, no 'cuh'. Formation is the anticlockwise curve that a, d, g and o all grow from — worth over-practising.

spreads.label: /k/ as in kit
spreads.note: cat and cot are contrast words: same sound, different spelling.
spreads.errors: Same sound as c, so expect wrong-letter choices when spelling for a long time (kat). Useful pattern to drop in early: k likes to come before i and e (kit, kid). Formation: tall down-stroke, then the two arms.

spreads.label: /k/ as in sock
spreads.errors: Two letters, one sound — and it only ever ends a word or syllable, straight after a short vowel (sock, kick). Children write single k or c instead; drill the -ck ending pattern. One sound button under the pair.

spreads.label: /e/ as in pet
spreads.errors: e/i is the classic short-vowel confusion (pen/pin) — exaggerate the mouth shapes and keep minimal-pair games running all half-term. Formation: across first, then round.

spreads.label: /u/ as in up
dictation: The duck sat in the mud.
spreads.errors: u/o confusion in both directions (cup/cop). In writing, n/u inversions are common — u goes 'down, round, up, then down again'. Keep /u/ short: up, not 'yoo'.

spreads.label: /r/ as in run
dictation: The rat ran up the rock.
spreads.errors: /r/ is one of the last sounds to mature: many children say /w/ ('wabbit') until 6 or 7. Model back, never correct harshly. Keep it a growl — /rrr/, not 'ruh'.

spreads.label: /h/ as in hat
dictation: The hen hid in the hut.
spreads.errors: A whispered puff of air — the only English sound with no voice at all, so it cannot be held or sung. Children drop it in speech ('at' for hat); that is accent, not error. Tall ascender then bump.

spreads.label: /b/ as in bat
spreads.errors: The other half of the b/d reversal pair — it will confuse many children into Year 1 and a few into Year 2. Route beats shape: b is 'down the bat, then round the ball'. Also p/b voicing (b is the noisy one).

spreads.label: /f/ as in fan
spreads.errors: f/v voicing pair (fan/van — v is the noisy twin, arriving soon). Some children still say /f/ for /th/ ('fum' for thumb); age-typical until 6+. Continuous sound: teeth on lip, /fff/.

spreads.label: /f/ as in puff
spreads.errors: Double letters make ONE sound — children will try to say /f/ twice. Teach the spelling pattern: a short vowel followed by /f/ at the end of a word is written ff (off, puff). One sound button under both letters.

spreads.label: /l/ as in leg
dictation: The lid is on the pot.
I let the cat lick it.
spreads.errors: Many children say /w/ or /y/ for /l/ ('yeyow') — model, don't drill. Keep it continuous: /lll/ with the tongue tip up. Full-height ascender; an l that shrinks reads as i.

spreads.label: /l/ as in bell
dictation: The doll fell off the bed.
spreads.errors: Same rule as ff: short vowel + /l/ at the end = ll (bell, hill). Children who have just learned l will write one; praise the sound, teach the pattern. One button under the pair.

spreads.label: /s/ as in hiss
dictation: The mess is on the rug.
spreads.errors: Completes the double-letter set: short vowel + /s/ at the end = ss (miss, fuss). Contrast with the single s that ends plurals (cats) — a seed worth planting now, harvested at Level 4.

spreads.label: /j/ as in jam
dictation: The jam is in the jug.
Jack can jog to the hill.
spreads.errors: j/ch voicing pair (j is the noisy one). First true descender-with-a-dot: down below the line, curve, then dot last. English words never end in j — that fact becomes the dge rule at Level 6.

spreads.label: /v/ as in van
spreads.note: vest is CVCC — permitted by the Level 2 decodable rule.
dictation: The vet is in the van.
spreads.errors: f/v voicing pair — /v/ buzzes, /f/ whispers; feel the throat. English words never end in a bare v (there is always an e: have, give) — which is exactly why 'have' turns up as a tricky word at Level 5.

spreads.label: /w/ as in wig
dictation: The dog will wag a lot.
spreads.errors: Letter-name trouble: 'double-u' tells you nothing about /w/. Children who say /w/ for /r/ will now read both letters as the same sound — listen carefully in blending. Two sharp points, not rounded.

spreads.label: /ks/ as in box
dictation: The fox is in the box.
spreads.errors: The odd one out: one letter, two sounds (/k/+/s/). It never starts a word at this level — it lives at the end (box, six). Sound buttons: one button, and say both sounds crisply.

spreads.label: /y/ as in yes
spreads.errors: Letter name ('why') v sound /y/ — insist on the sound. At this level y is only ever a consonant at the start of words; its vowel jobs (by, very, gym) are Level 6 shifty work. Descender tail below the line.

spreads.label: /z/ as in zip
dictation: A zip is on the bag.
spreads.errors: s/z voicing pair — and the s at the end of 'is' and 'his' actually says /z/: the first shifty s children meet. Keep /z/ buzzing. Watch for s-shaped reversals when forming the zigzag.

levels.name: Special Friends
levels.gpcs_note: Plus Phase 4 adjacent-consonant drills (st sp bl cr str scr…) beginning here and continuing as a daily drill alongside L4a through Summer 1.
levels.decodable_rule: CVC, CVCC and CCVC words using all taught GPCs. Adjacent consonant clusters now permitted (e.g. stop, frog, crisp, stamp). Consonant digraphs in initial and final position.
exit_criteria: Reads all consonant digraphs (sh, ch, th, ng, nk, qu, zz) at sight
Reads the 12 cumulative tricky words at sight
Blends CCVC, CVCC and CCVCC words with consonant clusters
Writes a sentence using a capital letter, finger spaces and full stop consistently
Begins to use a question mark appropriately

term_map.teach: sh nk ch th ng qu zz · he she we me be · Phase 4 adjacent-consonant drills begin (st sp bl cr str scr…)
term_map.secure: Digraphs secure; adjacent-consonant work continues as a daily drill alongside L4a through Summer 1; question mark met

spreads.label: /sh/ as in ship
dictation: The fish is in the dish.
spreads.errors: The first special friends: two letters, one sound — children will try to sound s-h separately for a while. s/sh articulation pairs (sip/ship, sock/shock) are the drill. One dash under the digraph, not two dots.

spreads.label: /nk/ as in pink
spreads.errors: The hidden /n/ is the problem — children hear 'pik' and write pik for pink. Stretch the word slowly (p-i-nk) so the nose sound surfaces. Only ever after a short vowel at the end of a word or syllable.

spreads.label: /ch/ as in chip
dictation: The chick is in the shed.
spreads.errors: ch/sh confusion (chip/ship) in both reading and speech, plus the j/ch voicing pair. Keep /ch/ a crisp sneeze of a sound. Children who met 'sh' first may write it by default — sorting games fix this.

spreads.label: /th/ as in this and thin
spreads.errors: One spelling, two sounds: voiced th (this, them — the throat buzzes) and unvoiced th (thin, moth — a whisper). Do not labour the difference with children; just model both. Expect /f/ and /v/ substitutions ('fin', 'wiv') — age-typical to 6+.

spreads.label: /ng/ as in ring
spreads.errors: One back-of-the-mouth sound, not /n/ + /g/ — children add a hard 'g' ('sing-g') or drop the n in spelling ('sig'). It never starts an English word; it lives at the ends (ring) and before -ing forever after.

spreads.label: /kw/ as in quick
spreads.errors: Like x, this is two sounds in one spelling: /k/+/w/. q never goes out without u in English — say 'q and u stick together' every time. Children may write kw (kwik); praise the ear, correct the spelling.

spreads.label: /z/ as in buzz
spreads.note: This is the complete zz family at this level — a tiny but noisy set.
spreads.errors: Completes the doubling set from Level 2: short vowel + /z/ at the end = zz (buzz, fizz). One sound, one button under both letters. Watch the z reversal returning under speed.

spreads.label: adjacent consonants (Phase 4)
spreads.note: Not a new sound — two known sounds side by side. Drill daily from now until the end of Summer 1, alongside the Level 4 digraphs.
dictation: The frog is on the twig.
spreads.errors: Children drop the second consonant ('top' for stop, 'fog' for frog) or the first ('nes' for nest). Slow-blend every single phoneme — s-t-o-p — and use the sound buttons: four dots, no dashes. This is a blending skill, not a new GPC.

levels.name: Longer Sounds
levels.gpcs_note: These are our primary spellings for each sound. The alternatives (ai, oa, ur, ow-as-cow, oi) arrive at Levels 5-6 as 'same sound, different spelling'. The first Shifty Sounds appear this level.
levels.decodable_rule: Words using all taught GPCs including vowel digraphs and the trigraph igh. Two-syllable decodable words introduced.
exit_criteria: Reads all 12 Set 2 vowel digraphs and the 19 cumulative tricky words at sight
Blends two-syllable words with digraphs
Writes a sentence using 'and' to join two ideas
Uses question mark and exclamation mark appropriately
Forms letters with consistent size relative to the line

term_map.teach: ay ee igh ow(blow) oo(zoo) oo(look) · was my you they
term_map.secure: First vowel digraphs read in words and captions

term_map.teach: ar or air ir ou oy · her all are · plural -s/-es · -ing/-ed/-er (read, not spelled — spelling returns in L5c) · first Shifty Sounds appear
term_map.secure: All Phase 3 vowel digraphs; two-syllable decodable words; exit = ELG-consistent reader

spreads.label: /ai/ as in day
spreads.errors: ay is the end-of-word spelling of /ai/ (day, play) — children will meet ai (rain) at Level 5, so anchor the position rule now. Watch b/d creeping back into 'day' under the excitement of a new digraph.

spreads.label: /ee/ as in see
dictation: I can see the green tree.
spreads.errors: The friendliest digraph — errors are mostly in spelling, where children write one e for the long sound ('gren'). The ee/ea choice arrives at Level 5; until then ee is the default and that is fine.

spreads.label: /igh/ as in night
spreads.errors: Three letters, one sound — the first trigraph, and it feels like magic. One dash under all three. igh almost always comes before t (night, light); 'high' and 'sigh' are the outliers. Spelling attempts like 'lite' are honest phonics — praise, then show the pattern.

spreads.label: /oa/ as in snow
spreads.errors: ow says /oa/ here (blow the snow). The very same letters will say /ow/ as in cow at Level 6 — the classic shifty pair. Do not pre-teach the second sound; just anchor this one hard with the snow words.

spreads.label: /oo/ as in zoo
dictation: We got food at the zoo.
spreads.errors: Long oo — the owl sound. Its twin (short oo, next session) uses identical letters, so word-sorting (moon v book) is the core activity for the fortnight. Reading errors here are almost always the wrong twin, not a wrong sound.

spreads.label: /u/ as in book (short oo)
spreads.errors: Same spelling, second sound — say 'try it long, try it short, the word will tell you'. Helpful tendency (not a rule): oo before k is usually short (book, look, took). This is the children's first taste of flexible decoding.

spreads.label: /ar/ as in car
dictation: The car is in the park.
It is dark at the farm.
spreads.errors: The r changes the vowel — 'bossy r'. Children spell what they say and drop the r ('dak'), or read a-r as two sounds. One dash under ar every time. Doctor-style 'ah' anchors it.

spreads.label: /or/ as in fork
spreads.errors: Second bossy-r spelling. Letter-order reversals ('ro' for or) are common in early writing. aw will arrive at Level 5 making the same sound — enjoy having only one spelling for now.

spreads.label: /air/ as in chair
dictation: The chair is at the fair.
spreads.errors: A trigraph — three letters, one dash, one sound. Children who autopilot 'a-i-r' need the card flashed until it is one unit. The homophones (fair/fare, pair/pear) can wait; if a child spots one, celebrate it.

spreads.label: /ur/ as in bird
dictation: The bird sits in the dirt.
spreads.errors: ir is our default /er/ spelling at this level — ur and er join the family at Level 6 (until then 'her' is handled as a tricky word). The classic slip is letter order: 'gril' for girl, 'brid' for bird.

spreads.label: /ow/ as in out
spreads.errors: The 'ouch' sound. ou almost never ends an English word — that job belongs to ow-as-cow, arriving at Level 6. If a child reads ou as /oo/ (soup-style), that is a real Shifty Sound they have spotted early.

spreads.label: /oy/ as in boy
spreads.errors: Position rule worth teaching explicitly: oy at the end of a word or syllable (boy, enjoy), and its partner oi (Level 5) in the middle (coin). Plant it now and the Level 5 session lands in minutes.

levels.name: New Spellings
levels.phase: Phase 5 (split digraphs + first alternatives) / RWI early Set 3
levels.gpcs_note: The teaching approach from here is 'same sound, different spelling' — /ai/ can be spelled ay (day), a-e (cake) or ai (rain). Spring 2 is a whole-code revision half-term (see the PSC preparation page).
levels.decodable_rule: All previously taught GPCs plus split digraphs and first alternative spellings. Multi-syllable words increasingly common.
exit_criteria: Reads split digraphs and first alternative spellings fluently
Reads multi-syllable decodable words
Reads all 33 cumulative tricky words at sight
Writes 2-3 connected sentences in sequence
Applies -ing, -ed, -er suffixes correctly to short roots
Ready for the Phonics Screening Check

term_map.teach: Split digraphs a-e i-e o-e u-e · said so have like
ea ie oi aw ai oa · some come were there little one
term_map.secure: 'Same sound, different spelling' mindset; multi-syllable words routine

term_map.teach: do when out what · suffixes with root change (hop→hopping) · prefix un- · commas in lists
term_map.secure: Full L5 code; sentences sequenced into short narratives

term_map.teach: Whole-code revision L1-L5 · daily alien-word fluency · gap-fill from tracker · er ur ow(cow) ear ure taught as read-only graphemes
term_map.secure: Every child reading real + alien words across the full assessable code, including the five read-only PSC graphemes

spreads.label: /ai/ as in cake (split digraph)
dictation: I made a cake for Dad.
He came late to the gate.
spreads.errors: The a and the e work as a team around one consonant — call it a split digraph and draw the joining arc. Early errors: reading 'cak-eh' (sounding the e) and spelling 'caik' (reaching for the Level 4/5 digraphs). Both are signs of good phonics, not bad.

spreads.label: /igh/ as in bike (split digraph)
dictation: I like to ride my bike.
He can smile all the time.
spreads.errors: Reading 'bik' (missing the e's long-distance job) is the main slip — cover the middle consonant to show the team. Spelling choice v igh: a helpful lean is igh before t (night, light), i-e elsewhere (bike, five).

spreads.label: /oa/ as in home (split digraph)
dictation: The dog dug up a bone.
spreads.errors: The /oa/ family now has two members (ow-as-snow, o-e) with oa itself still to come — start a sound wall and sort by position. Watch children writing 'hoam' or 'howm': right sound, wrong choice — the sort fixes it.

spreads.label: /yoo/ and /oo/ as in cube and flute
dictation: I like the tune on the flute.
spreads.errors: One spelling, two close sounds: /yoo/ (cube, cute) and /oo/ (flute, rude). Accept either in reading — the word decides. Sorting the two piles as a class settles it in a session.

spreads.label: /ee/ as in sea
dictation: The team went to the beach.
spreads.errors: The first big alternative: ee and ea sound identical, and the choice is unpredictable — expect spelling swaps ('cleen', 'sleap') for a year or more; keep the word sorts running. The shifty ea (bread, head) belongs to the Shifty Sounds strand — when a child meets it, try long, then short.

spreads.label: /igh/ as in pie
spreads.errors: A tiny family — pie, tie, lie — plus the -ied/-ies forms of try, cry and fly, which is where children will actually meet it. If a child reads ie as /ee/ (as in 'field'), that is the shifty twin: acknowledge and move on.

spreads.label: /oy/ as in coin
dictation: The coin was in the soil.
spreads.errors: The position rule planted at Level 4 completes: oi in the middle (coin, join), oy at the end (boy, enjoy). Spelling 'joyn' means the rule needs re-saying, not that the sound is insecure.

spreads.label: /or/ as in saw
dictation: I saw the hawk at dawn.
spreads.errors: Same sound as or — the first /or/ alternative, so spelling-choice errors ('sor' for saw) begin here. aw is fond of word endings (saw, draw, straw). Reading is rarely the problem; choice is.

spreads.label: /ai/ as in rain
dictation: The train was in the rain.
spreads.errors: Third spelling of /ai/: ai in the middle (rain), ay at the end (day), a-e around a consonant (cake). Wrong-choice spellings are normal for a year — that is exactly what the weekly word sort is for. Reading should be instant by now.

spreads.label: /oa/ as in boat
dictation: The goat is on the boat.
There was soap on the road.
spreads.errors: Completes the /oa/ trio: oa in the middle (boat), ow at the end (snow), o-e around a consonant (bone). By now children read all three without blinking; the work is all in choosing when writing — sort, sort, sort.

levels.name: Building Fluency
levels.phase: Phase 5 continued (more alternatives + consonant alternatives) / RWI Set 3 continued
levels.gpcs_note: Additional graphemes in worksheet word pools (no dedicated book): oe (toe), au (cause), e-e (these), c as /s/ (city), sc as /s/ (science). Alternative pronunciations of known graphemes are also taught: a (cat/acorn/want), e (bed/he), i (pin/find), o (hot/cold), u (cup/unit/put), y (yes/by/very/gym), ow (now/blow), ch (chip/chef/school).
levels.decodable_rule: Full Phase 5 GPC repertoire including consonant alternatives and alternative pronunciations. Multi-syllable words standard.
exit_criteria: Reads alternative spellings and pronunciations fluently
Reads consonant alternatives (wr, kn, ge, dge, mb, gn, ph, wh)
Reads multi-syllable words including suffixes
Writes the four sentence types correctly
Uses expanded noun phrases in own writing
Uses apostrophes for contractions
Begins joining handwriting consistently

term_map.teach: Screening Check window · then ur er are ow(brown) ew ue
term_map.secure: Phonics Screening Check (L5 exit criterion: 'ready for the PSC')

term_map.teach: wr kn ge/dge · four sentence forms · coordination (and/but/or/so)
term_map.secure: First alternative consonant spellings; post-check momentum kept

term_map.teach: mb gn ph wh + word-pool graphemes (oe au e-e, soft c, sc) · their people could
term_map.secure: Full L6 code; expanded noun phrases; subordination

spreads.label: /ur/ as in turn
dictation: We surf when the sun is out.
spreads.errors: Third spelling of /er/ (after ir at Level 4). There is no reliable rule for ir/ur — build word banks instead: nurse, church, burn take ur. Reading is easy; expect spelling swaps ('hirt') and sort them without drama.

spreads.label: /er/ as in letter
dictation: My sister sent her a letter.
We had dinner in the summer.
spreads.errors: er owns the lazy, unstressed ending of two-syllable words (better, summer) — the schwa. Children spell what they hear and write 'betta'. And 'her', a tricky word since Level 4, is suddenly decodable: point this out — children love the promotion.

spreads.label: /air/ as in care
dictation: The hare gave me a stare.
spreads.errors: Same letters as the tricky word 'are' — but a different job: at the end of these words the trio says /air/. Expect double-takes for a week. Second /air/ spelling after air (chair); word-bank it, don't rule it.

spreads.label: /ow/ as in cow (second sound of ow)
dictation: The clown is in town now.
spreads.errors: The shifty pair completes: ow says /ow/ (cow) as well as /oa/ (snow, from Level 4). The strategy is the Level 6 super-skill — try both sounds and let the word decide. Books mark the shifted sound with the shifty diamond; the grey shifty card carries both.

spreads.label: /oo/ and /yoo/ as in grew and few
spreads.errors: Like u-e, this spelling carries /oo/ (grew) and /yoo/ (few) — accept either, sort as a class. The /oo/ family is now three spellings strong and growing; the running word wall matters more than any rule.

spreads.label: /oo/ and /yoo/ as in blue and rescue
spreads.errors: ue likes to end the word (blue, rescue, statue). With ew, u-e and oo, the /oo/ sound now has four spellings — run the sort weekly and keep spelling expectations kind. Reading errors are rare by this stage.

spreads.label: /r/ as in write (silent w)
spreads.errors: The first silent letter: say /r/, ignore the w. Children sound the /w/ for months when spelling aloud — anchor with 'you write with your wrist'. A small, learnable family; treat it as vocabulary as much as phonics.

spreads.label: /n/ as in knee (silent k)
dictation: She knows how to tie a knot.
spreads.errors: Silent k — an Old English fossil (it was once pronounced!). knight/night and knew/new are gift homophones for a sorting game. Reading clicks fast; spelling 'nee' for knee lingers — word-family practice beats correction.

spreads.label: /j/ as in page and bridge (soft g)
spreads.errors: English words never end in j (planted at Level 2) — this is why. After a short vowel use dge (badge, fudge); after anything else use ge (page, huge). One of the few spelling rules that almost always works, so teach it as a rule.

spreads.label: /m/ as in lamb (silent b)
dictation: The lamb is with its mum.
spreads.errors: Silent b at word ends. Children sound the /b/ when reading ('lam-buh') and drop the letter when spelling — both fade with word-family work. climb is also on the Y2 word list at Level 7: double exposure is deliberate.

spreads.label: /n/ as in gnome (silent g)
dictation: A gnome sat by the sign.
The rat will gnaw the rope.
spreads.errors: Silent g, tiny family: gnat, gnaw, gnome, sign. A lovely morphology seed: the g in sign comes back to life in signal — worth thirty seconds of wonder. Otherwise treat as sight-familiar vocabulary.

spreads.label: /f/ as in phone
dictation: I spoke to Gran on the phone.
The elephant is in the photo.
spreads.errors: ph = /f/, mostly in words borrowed from Greek (phone, photo, graph). Reading is easy; the f/ph spelling choice is not — keep a Greek-words poster growing on the wall. Children may over-apply it ('phun').

spreads.label: /w/ as in wheel
spreads.errors: wh = /w/ in our accent — no need for a breathy 'hw'. The question words cluster here (when, which, why, what): link to question-mark work. 'when' and 'what', tricky words since Level 5, are now decodable — another promotion to celebrate.

levels.name: Reading Together
levels.phase: Late Phase 5 (trigraphs + complex endings) / RWI Grey 9-11
levels.gpcs_note: Phase 6 morphology is introduced alongside: suffixes -s -es -ing -ed -er -est -y -en -ful -ly -ment -ness, the doubling rule, the drop-e rule, y→i, past tense of regular and irregular verbs, contractions and possessive apostrophes. Alien words are retired from this level.
levels.tricky_label: Common Exception Words (NC Y2 list, first set)
levels.decodable_rule: Full Phase 5 GPC repertoire including trigraphs. Complex sentence structures expected.
exit_criteria: Reads trigraphs (ire, ore, ear, oor, ure) and tion fluently
Reads fluently with expression and intonation
Spells CEWs from the Y2 list accurately
Applies suffix rules in independent writing
Writes a sequenced recount or short narrative with time adverbials
Uses contractions and possessive apostrophes correctly
Handwriting is consistently joined and legible

term_map.teach: ire ore ear oor ure tion · Y2 CEWs begin
Phase 6 suffix rules: doubling, drop-e, y→i · -ful -ly -ment -ness · homophones
term_map.secure: Suffix spelling rules applied in writing; CEW set 1 to mastery

spreads.label: /igh-er/ as in fire
dictation: We sat by the fire because it was cold.
spreads.errors: A trigraph that can feel like two beats (fi-re) — either is fine; keep the blend smooth. Spelling attempts like 'fiyer' show good ears; show the three-letter team. Often lands inside longer words (bonfire, admire) — a chance to practise syllable chunking.

spreads.label: /or/ as in more
dictation: He told me the score before the end.
spreads.errors: The /or/ family grows again: or, aw, now ore — and door/floor arrive next session. ore usually ends the word (more, score, before). Spelling choice, not reading, is the work: sort by position and keep the wall chart honest.

spreads.label: /eer/ as in near
spreads.errors: ear says /eer/ here — but the same letters say /er/ in learn and /air/ in bear: a triple shifty, diamond-marked in the books. Try /eer/ first; let the word decide. hear/here is the homophone to tackle head-on ('you hear with your ear').

spreads.label: /or/ as in door
dictation: The poor dog sat by the door.
The toys are on the floor.
spreads.errors: A tiny family — door, floor, poor, moor — and all three of the big ones are also on the Y2 word list, so the double exposure is deliberate. Children spell 'dor'; the word wall and spelling tests carry this one.

spreads.label: /ure/ as in picture
dictation: We drew a picture of the adventure.
spreads.errors: After t, ure usually softens to /cher/ (picture, adventure) — accept both pronunciations. 'sure' (and 'sugar') start with /sh/ — both live on the word lists as exceptions. A rich harvest of grown-up words: treat the list as vocabulary teaching too.

spreads.label: /shun/ as in station
spreads.errors: The workhorse ending of written English — always an unstressed final syllable, so clap the syllables before blending. Children spell 'shun' or 'sion'; the -sion cousins arrive at Level 8, so for now tion is the only correct choice. Never split it: one unit, one dash.

levels.name: Reading Champion
levels.gpcs_note: Children are now reading for meaning rather than learning new grapheme-phoneme correspondences. The 'GPCs' of this level are morphemes — suffixes and prefixes that unlock multi-syllable vocabulary. Suffix and root changes are explicit teaching points.
levels.tricky_label: Common Exception Words (NC Y2 list, remaining)
levels.decodable_rule: Full Phase 5 GPC repertoire plus Phase 6 morphology. Suffix and root changes are explicit teaching points.
exit_criteria: Reads age-appropriate text fluently and with comprehension
Spells Y2 CEWs to mastery
Writes a multi-paragraph piece with sentence variety
Edits own writing for accuracy
Ready for Y3 curriculum

term_map.teach: -ous -cious -tious -able -ible · re- dis- mis- · reading for meaning
term_map.secure: Morphology opens multi-syllable vocabulary; inference discussed

term_map.teach: -tion/-sion families · remaining Y2 CEWs · sentence variety, fronted adverbials
Fluency, stamina, editing/proofreading · Y3-readiness (inverted commas met)
term_map.secure: Exit = fluent independent reader; programme complete

spreads.label: /us/ as in famous ('full of')
dictation: It is dangerous to climb the enormous rock.
spreads.errors: -ous turns a noun into an adjective meaning 'full of' (danger → dangerous). The vowel is an unstressed schwa, so children spell 'famus' or 'famess'. British spelling watch: marvellous keeps its double l.

spreads.label: /uh-bl/ as in enjoyable
dictation: The trip was enjoyable and remarkable.
spreads.errors: -able is the default choice (it is far more common than -ible). The working test: if you can hear a complete root word, choose -able (enjoy → enjoyable, wash → washable). The a is a schwa — children write '-ubble' and '-ible' freely; keep the rule visible.

spreads.label: /uh-bl/ as in sensible
spreads.errors: -ible follows roots that cannot stand alone (horr-, poss-, incred-). Say the rule, then expect errors anyway — this pair trips up adults. Build the two class lists side by side and let frequency do the teaching.

spreads.label: /shus/ as in delicious
dictation: Her precious ring was in a spacious box.
spreads.errors: -cious = /shus/. The choosing rule: if the root ends in -ce (space → spacious, grace → gracious), take -cious. Clap the syllables first — these are three- and four-beat words and the ending is always the quiet beat.

spreads.label: /shus/ as in cautious
spreads.note: The complete -tious family at this level — a small, high-value set.
spreads.errors: Also /shus/ — the twin of -cious. The choosing rule: if there is a related -tion word (caution → cautious, ambition → ambitious), take -tious. Teach the two endings in the same week so the contrast does the work.

spreads.label: prefixes ('again', 'not', 'wrongly', 'under')
dictation: Refill the jug and return it.
spreads.errors: Prefixes bolt on without changing the root's spelling — dis + appear keeps both letters (disappear), mis + spell keeps both s's. Children double or drop letters at the seam; write the two parts in two colours and physically push them together.

spreads.label: /shun/ and /zhun/ as in station and television
spreads.errors: The -sion cousins finally arrive: -sion says /zhun/ after a vowel (division, explosion) and /shun/ after l, n or r (mansion, version). Sort by the sound you hear first; the spelling follows. -tion remains the default when in doubt.
